explanation: The infraorbital nerve (V2) carries pain sensation from the lower eyelid, upper lip, and cheek, exiting through the infraorbital foramen on the anterior maxilla.
keyConcept: Lower eyelid pain: infraorbital nerve (V2).

explanation: The submental lymph nodes drain the chin and lower lip midline, lying beneath the chin in the submental triangle.
keyConcept: Chin infection: submental lymph nodes enlarge.

explanation: The falx cerebri is the dural fold attached to the skull vault along the midline, lying between the cerebral hemispheres with its anterior attachment at the crista galli.
keyConcept: Falx cerebri: dural fold attached to skull vault.

explanation: The anterior and posterior ethmoidal arteries (from the ophthalmic artery) give off anterior meningeal arteries that supply the cranial dura in the anterior fossa.
keyConcept: Ethmoidal arteries supply dura via anterior meningeal branches.

explanation: The middle meningeal artery enters the cranial cavity through foramen spinosum (not ovale), making it vulnerable to fractures in the temporal region causing epidural hematoma.
keyConcept: Middle meningeal artery: enters via foramen spinosum, not ovale.

explanation: The abducent nerve (CN VI) runs through the cavernous sinus adjacent to the internal carotid artery; an aneurysm here compresses CN VI causing lateral rectus palsy.
keyConcept: Cavernous ICA aneurysm compresses abducent nerve (CN VI).

explanation: The facial nerve (CN VII) does not pass through the cavernous sinus; it exits via stylomastoid foramen, so it wouldn't be affected in cavernous sinus thrombosis.
keyConcept: Facial nerve not in cavernous sinus, so not tested in thrombosis.

explanation: The superior petrosal sinus drains the cavernous sinus into the transverse sinus, running along the petrous ridge at the attachment of tentorium cerebelli.
keyConcept: Cavernous sinus drains to transverse sinus via superior petrosal sinus.

explanation: The straight sinus deviates to the LEFT to continue as the left transverse sinus (not right); the right transverse sinus typically continues from the superior sagittal sinus.
keyConcept: Straight sinus deviates LEFT to become left transverse sinus.

explanation: The frontal diploic vein drains through the supraorbital notch to the supraorbital vein and eventually the angular vein, providing extracranial drainage.
keyConcept: Frontal diploic vein drains extracranially via supraorbital vein.

explanation: Subdural hemorrhage crosses suture lines because it's venous bleeding with low pressure that accumulates slowly, unlike arterial extradural bleeding which is confined by suture attachments.
keyConcept: Subdural bleeding crosses suture lines (venous).

explanation: The common facial vein drains into the internal jugular vein, not the external jugular. The external jugular tributaries are anterior jugular, transverse cervical, suprascapular, and posterior external jugular.
keyConcept: Common facial vein drains internal jugular, not external jugular.

explanation: The external jugular vein is the only named tributary of the subclavian vein, carrying blood from the superficial structures of the head and neck.
keyConcept: External jugular vein: only named tributary of subclavian vein.

explanation: The pretracheal fascia forms a sheath around the trachea, esophagus, and thyroid gland, fusing laterally with the carotid sheath.
keyConcept: Pretracheal fascia surrounds cervical viscera.

explanation: The retropharyngeal space lies between the buccopharyngeal fascia (covering pharynx/esophagus) anteriorly and prevertebral fascia posteriorly, extending from skull base to T1.
keyConcept: Retropharyngeal space: between buccopharyngeal and prevertebral fascia.

explanation: The axillary sheath is an extension of the prevertebral fascia (from the anterior vertebral muscles) that surrounds the axillary vessels and brachial plexus.
keyConcept: Axillary sheath: extension of prevertebral fascia.

explanation: The thyrohyoid muscle is innervated directly by C1 fibers via the hypoglossal nerve, while other infrahyoid muscles receive ansa cervicalis (C1-3).
keyConcept: Thyrohyoid: directly by C1 via hypoglossal nerve.

explanation: The facial artery runs through both carotid triangle (origin from ECA) and digastric triangle (before entering face), giving off branches like submental, superior labial, and lateral nasal.
keyConcept: Facial artery: runs through both carotid and digastric triangles.

explanation: The carotid sheath contains the common/internal carotid artery, internal jugular vein, and vagus nerve throughout its course in the neck.
keyConcept: Carotid sheath: contains CCA/ICA, IJV, and vagus nerve.

explanation: The lesser occipital nerve runs along the posterior border of sternocleidomastoid muscle, arising from C2 ventral ramus to supply the scalp behind the ear.
keyConcept: Lesser occipital nerve: posterior border of SCM.

explanation: The anterior scalene muscle divides the subclavian artery into three parts: first (posterior to scalene), second (behind scalene), and third (lateral to scalene).
keyConcept: Subclavian artery divided by anterior scalene muscle into 3 parts.

explanation: The spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) crosses the posterior triangle embedded in its roof, running from the sternocleidomastoid to the trapezius, parallel to levator scapulae.
keyConcept: Spinal accessory nerve: crosses posterior triangle parallel to levator scapulae.

explanation: Tight scalene muscles (especially anterior and middle) can compress the subclavian artery and brachial plexus in the costoclavicular space, causing thoracic outlet syndrome.
keyConcept: Scalene tightness compresses subclavian artery.

explanation: The phrenic nerve runs on the anterior surface of the anterior scalene muscle, making it vulnerable during scalene blocks and relevant in interscalene anesthesia.
keyConcept: Phrenic nerve: anterior aspect of anterior scalene muscle.

explanation: The rectus capitis posterior minor does NOT form boundaries of the suboccipital triangle - only rectus capitis posterior major, obliquus capitis superior, and obliquus capitis inferior do.
keyConcept: Suboccipital triangle: rectus major, obliquus superior/inferior (NOT rectus minor).

explanation: The dorsal ramus of C1 (suboccipital nerve) emerges in the floor of the suboccipital triangle, providing motor innervation to suboccipital muscles.
keyConcept: Suboccipital triangle floor: dorsal ramus of C1.

explanation: The auriculotemporal nerve lies superficial to the temporalis fascia as it ascends toward the temple, carrying sensory fibers from the mandibular nerve.
keyConcept: Auriculotemporal nerve: superficial to temporalis fascia.

explanation: The temporalis muscle is a powerful retractor of the mandible, pulling the mandibular condyle backward to close the mouth after opening.
keyConcept: Temporalis: powerful retractor of mandible.

explanation: The lateral pterygoid is the main mouth opener, pulling the mandibular neck forward and down; gravity and suprahyoid muscles assist.
keyConcept: Lateral pterygoid: main opener of mouth.

explanation: The mandibular nerve (V3) passes from the middle cranial fossa to the infratemporal fossa through foramen ovale.
keyConcept: Mandibular nerve enters infratemporal fossa through foramen ovale.

explanation: The trunk of the mandibular nerve gives off medial pterygoid nerve (supplying medial pterygoid, tensor tympani, and tensor palati) before dividing into anterior and posterior divisions.
keyConcept: V3 trunk supplies: medial pterygoid, tensor tympani, tensor palati.

explanation: The auriculotemporal nerve encircles the middle meningeal artery with its two roots, forming a neural loop around the vessel in the infratemporal fossa.
keyConcept: Auriculotemporal nerve encircles middle meningeal artery.

explanation: Bad extraction of lower third molar can damage the inferior alveolar nerve (running in the mandibular canal), causing anesthesia of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.
keyConcept: Lower 3rd molar extraction: possible lingual nerve damage (anterior 2/3 tongue).

explanation: The inferior alveolar nerve (branch of V3) is anesthetized for lower teeth operations, injected near the mandibular foramen on the medial aspect of the ramus.
keyConcept: Lower teeth surgery: inferior alveolar nerve anesthetized.

explanation: The posterior superior alveolar artery is a branch of the third part of maxillary artery that supplies the upper molars and sinuses.
keyConcept: Posterior superior alveolar artery: branch of maxillary artery part 3.

explanation: The buccal nerve passes between the two heads of the lateral pterygoid muscle to reach the buccinator muscle, carrying sensory and motor fibers.
keyConcept: Buccal nerve passes between two heads of lateral pterygoid.
